mainTopic: Using the משנה of כלים וקרקעות to settle whether a claim for two different types, where the defendant admits one type and denies the other, requires an oath; and the question of why the משנה would teach זקיקה when it is already taught elsewhere.
overview: The amud asks what happens when someone claims two different kinds of items and the defendant admits one kind and denies the other. The גמרא tries to prove from the משנה of כלים וקרקעות that such a defendant must swear. It answers that the משנה mentions land to teach זקיקה, and that our משנה is the main source for that rule. רבי חייא בר אבא quotes רבי יוחנן that wheat and barley are exempt. Proofs against him from the משנה and from an ox-and-sheep ברייתא are turned aside, and the ברייתא is finally assigned to אדמון, as a set tradition of רבי יוחנן. Then come rulings of רב ענן in the name of שמואל about a defendant who jumps in with a trick and about two needles. Next is רב פפא's case of vessels and a פרוטה, which the גמרא explains as following רב on one point and שמואל on the other. Last, רב נחמן rules that someone who denies the whole claim still swears a שבועת היסת. The גמרא defends this with the idea that a borrower may only be stalling, and then brings רב חביבא's version, which attaches the oath to the later case of the משנה.

steps.title: End of the משנה about vessels and land
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes quoting a משנה: admitting part of the land claim means no oath, but admitting part of the vessels claim means an oath is required.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he admitted to part of the land, he is exempt. If he admitted to part of the vessels, he is liable to take an oath.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is quoting the last lines of a משנה about a claim for both vessels and land. This sets up an inference the גמרא is about to draw.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is no oath for claims about land (קרקעות), so admitting part of the land claim brings no oath. Admitting part of the vessels claim is a real מודה במקצת on movable items, so he must swear.

keyTerms.meaning: admitted to part of the claim

phrases.english: If he admitted to part of the land, he is exempt.
If he admitted to part of the vessels, he is liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the quotation of the משנה that the גמרא began citing just before this point.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Partial admission on land does not bring an oath; partial admission on vessels does.

steps.title: Inferring that two kinds of vessels would require an oath
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא infers that the exemption in the משנה is only because land has no oath. So if the claim were for two kinds of vessels, and he admitted one kind and denied the other, he would be liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: The reason he is exempt is that the claim was vessels and land, and land is not subject to an oath. But if it were vessels and vessels, like the case of vessels and land, he would be liable!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws an inference from the משנה to prove that admitting one type while denying another type requires an oath.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the earlier part of the משנה, he admitted the vessels and denied the land, and was exempt. The גמרא says the only reason is that land never gets an oath. So in the same setup with two kinds of movables, he should be liable.

keyTerms.meaning: similar to, in the same setup as

phrases.english: The reason is that it was vessels and land,
since land is not subject to an oath;
but vessels and vessels,
phrases.notes: He means two different kinds of vessels: he admits owing one kind and denies the other.

phrases.english: in the same setup as vessels and land, he is liable!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws a דיוק from the quoted משנה.
steps.raayaObject: That admitting one type and denying another type obligates an oath.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה exempts in the vessels-and-land case only because land has no oath.

steps.title: Maybe two kinds of vessels are also exempt
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the inference. Perhaps two kinds of vessels would also be exempt. The משנה chose land to teach that an oath on the vessels pulls the land into the oath too.
steps.simpleTranslation: The same is true even for vessels and vessels: he is also exempt. The reason the משנה teaches vessels and land is to tell us that when he admits part of the vessels, he must swear about the land too.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the proof by giving a different reason why the משנה mentioned land.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The inference only works if the choice of land was meant to explain the exemption. The גמרא suggests land was chosen for a different lesson: זקיקה, meaning once he must swear about vessels, the land claim is attached to that oath. So the משנה tells us nothing about two kinds of vessels.

phrases.english: The same is true, that even
for vessels and vessels he is also exempt;
and the reason it teaches vessels and land
is to teach us
that when he admitted to part of the vessels,
he is liable to swear even about the land.

steps.triggerLanguage: הוּא הַדִּין דַּאֲפִילּוּ כֵּלִים וְכֵלִים נָמֵי פָּטוּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the inference of step 2 by giving another purpose for the משנה's wording.
steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not saying land claims now get their own oath. Land still has no oath. It is only pulled in because he already has to swear about the vessels.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the proof from the משנה, without deciding the law of two kinds of vessels.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The mention of land may serve to teach זקיקה, not to explain why he is exempt.

steps.title: זקיקה is already taught elsewhere
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the rejection. What new point would the משנה be teaching? זקיקה is already taught in a משנה (קידושין 26a), which says movables bind land so that he must swear about it.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is it teaching us? That movables bind land? We already learned: "They bind the property that has a guarantee, to swear about it"!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer in step 3, saying the rule of זקיקה is already known from another משנה, so it cannot be the reason for this משנה's wording.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A משנה is not supposed to repeat a rule that is already taught elsewhere. Since זקיקה is already stated in קידושין, the explanation in step 3 seems weak, and the original inference comes back into play. Step 5 answers this.

keyTerms.meaning: bind, attach (the land to the oath on the movables)
property that has a guarantee, meaning land

phrases.english: What is it teaching us? That they bind?!
We already learned: "They bind the property
phrases.notes: This is a משנה in קידושין 26a. The movables he must swear about are what do the binding.

phrases.english: that has a guarantee,
phrases.notes: Land is called property with a guarantee because a lender can collect from it.

phrases.english: to swear about it"!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the explanation of the משנה offered in step 3.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in step 3 that the משנה mentions land in order to teach זקיקה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: זקיקה is already stated in a משנה in קידושין, so this משנה would be repeating it for no reason.
steps.whyThisMatters: If this challenge holds, the דיוק from step 2 returns and would prove that admitting one type and denying another requires an oath.

steps.title: Our משנה is the main source and the other only mentions it in passing
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers the question from Step 4. Our משנה is the main place for זקיקה. The משנה in קידושין only brings it along with other rules.
steps.simpleTranslation: This משנה is the main one. That משנה brought it along incidentally.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why our משנה needs to teach זקיקה even though the משנה in קידושין already teaches it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Our משנה is about the laws of oaths, so this is the true home of זקיקה. The משנה in קידושין lists many differences between land and movables and mentions זקיקה only as part of that list. Because the repetition is now explained, Step 3's reading of the משנה still stands.

keyTerms.meaning: The main, primary place where a rule is taught
Incidentally; dragged along with something else

phrases.english: This one is the main source,
phrases.notes: "This one" is our משנה in שבועות, which is all about oaths.

phrases.english: that one brought it incidentally.
phrases.notes: "That one" is the משנה in קידושין from Step 4.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָא עִיקָּר, הָהִיא אַגַּב גְּרָרָא נַסְבַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 4 and protects the rejection made in Step 3.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since קידושין already teaches זקיקה, our משנה would add nothing by teaching it.
steps.terutzMaskana: Our משנה is the main source for זקיקה, and קידושין only mentions it along the way. Repeating it is fine.

steps.title: Claimed wheat and barley and admitted one of them, so he is exempt
steps.stepSummary: רבי חייא בר אבא quotes רבי יוחנן: if someone claims wheat and barley and the other admits one of them, there is no oath.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חייא בר אבא said in the name of רבי יוחנן: if he claimed wheat and barley from him and he admitted one of them, he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ruling about a claim for two different kinds, where the defendant admits one kind and denies the other.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is exactly the question Step 2 raised. Here רבי יוחנן rules that there is no oath. The admission does not count as admitting part of the same claim, because barley and wheat are separate claims.

keyTerms.meaning: Wheat and barley, two different kinds

phrases.aramaic: וְרַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: And Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba said that Rabbi Yoḥanan said:
If he claimed wheat and barley from him,
and he admitted to him one of them, he is exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new line that rules directly on the two-kinds case raised in Step 2.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A claim for two kinds where one kind is admitted does not require an oath.

steps.title: But רבי יוחנן was quoted as ruling there is an oath
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges Step 6. רבי יצחק praised the ruling that there is an oath and said that רבי יוחנן said the same.
steps.simpleTranslation: But didn't רבי יצחק say: "Well said, and so said רבי יוחנן"?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out a contradiction. Two reports of רבי יוחנן's view say opposite things.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יצחק approved the ruling that a defendant who admits one of two kinds must swear, and he said רבי יוחנן agrees. That clashes with רבי חייא בר אבא's report that רבי יוחנן exempts him.

keyTerms.meaning: But didn't (he) say? A formula that raises a contradiction

phrases.english: But didn't Rabbi Yitzḥak say: Well said,
phrases.notes: רבי יצחק is praising the ruling, said in the name of שמואל, that the defendant must swear in this case.

phrases.english: and so said Rabbi Yoḥanan!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָאָמַר רַבִּי יִצְחָק: יִישַׁר, וְכֵן אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the report of רבי יוחנן's view in Step 6.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי חייא בר אבא's report that רבי יוחנן exempts the defendant
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Another report says רבי יוחנן holds the defendant must swear, so both reports cannot be correct.

steps.title: Different אמוראים report רבי יוחנן differently
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that רבי חייא בר אבא and רבי יצחק are two אמוראים who disagree about what רבי יוחנן held.
steps.simpleTranslation: They are אמוראים, and they disagree about the view of רבי יוחנן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא resolves the contradiction. Two students simply heard or understood רבי יוחנן differently.
steps.deeperAnalysis: No one has to be forced into a new reading. The contradiction is real, and it is a disagreement between the reporters about what their teacher said.

keyTerms.meaning: They are (different) אמוראים, meaning they disagree
According to, regarding the view of

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a disagreement inside רבי יוחנן's own words. It is two later teachers reporting him in opposite ways.

phrases.english: They are amora'im
who disagree about the view of Rabbi Yoḥanan.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 7.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Dispute between reporters (אמוראים) about one teacher's view
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two reports contradict, so one of them must be wrong.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both reports are real. רבי חייא בר אבא and רבי יצחק disagree about רבי יוחנן's position.

steps.title: A proof from the משנה that wheat and barley would require an oath
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a משנה: claimed wheat and admitted barley is exempt. It infers that claiming both and admitting one would require an oath, which goes against רבי חייא בר אבא.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: if he claimed wheat and he admitted barley, he is exempt, and רבן גמליאל makes him liable. The reason is that he claimed only wheat and he admitted barley. But if he claimed wheat and barley and admitted one of them, he would be liable!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to prove from a משנה that admitting one of two claimed kinds requires an oath.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The exemption in the משנה seems to come from the fact that barley was never claimed at all. So if barley had been part of the claim, the admission would count and an oath would be needed. That would contradict Step 6.

keyTerms.meaning: The reason, used to make an inference

phrases.english: Come and hear:

phrases.aramaic: טְעָנוֹ חִטִּין וְהוֹדָה לוֹ בִּשְׂעוֹרִין – פָּטוּר,
phrases.english: If he claimed wheat and he admitted barley to him, he is exempt,
and Rabban Gamliel holds him liable.

phrases.aramaic: טַעְמָא דִּטְעָנוֹ חִטִּין וְהוֹדָה לוֹ בִּשְׂעוֹרִין;
phrases.english: The reason is that he claimed wheat and he admitted barley;
but if he claimed wheat and barley
and admitted one of them to him, he would be liable!

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: טְעָנוֹ חִטִּין וְהוֹדָה לוֹ בִּשְׂעוֹרִין – פָּטוּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses a משנה to argue against רבי חייא בר אבא's ruling in Step 6.
steps.raayaObject: Admitting one of two claimed kinds requires an oath
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה about claiming wheat and admitting barley, read through an inference from its wording

steps.title: The משנה's case shows how far רבן גמליאל goes
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof. Even wheat and barley might be exempt. The משנה used a claim of wheat alone to show that רבן גמליאל requires an oath even there.
steps.simpleTranslation: The same law could apply: even with wheat and barley he is also exempt. The reason it taught this case is to show you the strength of רבן גמליאל's view.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the inference. The משנה's choice of case is not meant to teach that wheat and barley requires an oath.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The חכמים could exempt in both cases. The משנה picked the weakest case for an oath, where barley was never claimed at all, to show that רבן גמליאל still requires an oath. So the proof against רבי חייא בר אבא fails.

keyTerms.meaning: To let you know the strength (how far-reaching) of his view

steps.whatToRemember: A משנה often picks an extreme case to show how far one opinion goes. Because of this, we cannot always infer the opposite rule from its exact case.
steps.whyThisMatters: The proof from the משנה is taken away, so the ruling of רבי חייא בר אבא in the name of רבי יוחנן still stands.

phrases.english: The same law applies, that even with wheat and barley
he is also exempt,
and the reason it teaches it this way
phrases.notes: "This way" means the case where only wheat was claimed.

phrases.english: is to let you know the strength of Rabban Gamliel's view.

steps.triggerLanguage: הוּא הַדִּין דַּאֲפִילּוּ חִטִּין וּשְׂעוֹרִין נָמֵי פָּטוּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the inference made in Step 9.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the inference only. The משנה's ruling itself stays in place.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The משנה's case was chosen to show how far רבן גמליאל goes, not to imply that wheat and barley would require an oath.

steps.title: A proof from the case of vessels and land
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a משנה about a claim of vessels and land. It infers that a claim of two kinds of vessels, where one kind is admitted, would require an oath. That goes against רבי חייא בר אבא.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: if he claimed vessels and land, and the other admitted the vessels and denied the land, or admitted the land and denied the vessels, he is exempt. If he admitted part of the land, he is exempt. If he admitted part of the vessels, he must swear. The reason he is exempt is that the claim was vessels and land, and land is not something you swear about. But a claim of vessels and other vessels, set up like the case of vessels and land, would require an oath!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries a new proof against רבי חייא בר אבא, using the משנה's case of vessels and land.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says there is no oath when someone claims vessels and land and the other admits only one of them. The גמרא reasons that the only reason for this is that land never gets an oath. So if both items were vessels (two different items, like wheat and barley), there would be an oath, which is the opposite of what רבי חייא בר אבא reported.

keyTerms.meaning: Something that can be the subject of an oath
Similar to, set up the same way

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think land is being excluded from monetary claims in general. The rule here is only that the Torah's oath for partial admission does not apply to land.

phrases.english: Come and hear:
If he claimed vessels and land from him,
and the other admitted the vessels and denied the land,
or admitted the land and denied the vessels: he is exempt.
If he admitted part of the land: he is exempt.
If he admitted part of the vessels: he must swear.
The reason is that it was vessels and land,
since land is not subject to an oath;
but vessels and other vessels,
set up like vessels and land: he must swear!
phrases.notes: He means: two different items claimed, and only one admitted, just like wheat and barley.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the proof in Step 9 was rejected, the גמרא tries another proof from the same משנה.
steps.raayaObject: That claiming two different items and admitting one requires an oath, against רבי חייא בר אבא's report of רבי יוחנן.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה about vessels and land, read through an inference: the exemption is only because land has no oath.

steps.title: The vessels-and-land case teaches something else
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof. Two kinds of vessels might also be exempt. The משנה used land to teach that admitting part of the vessels brings the land into the oath too.
steps.simpleTranslation: The same is true that even vessels and other vessels would be exempt. The משנה is teaching us that if he admitted part of the vessels, he must swear about the land too.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the proof and gives a different reason why the משנה mentioned land.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof assumed land was mentioned only to explain the exemption. The גמרא says no: two kinds of vessels could also be exempt, and land was mentioned for a new lesson. Once a person must swear about the vessels, the oath also covers the land.

phrases.english: The same is true that even
vessels and other vessels would also be exempt;
and this is what it teaches us:
that if he admitted part of the vessels,
he must swear about the land as well.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof of Step 11 by giving another reason the משנה mentioned land.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the inference. The משנה itself stands.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed land was mentioned only to explain the exemption. In fact it was mentioned to teach that land gets pulled into the oath.

steps.title: Isn't the pulling-in rule already taught elsewhere?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the משנה would need to teach that land is pulled into the oath. Another משנה already teaches this.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is it teaching us? That property is pulled in? We already learned: movable property pulls in property that serves as a guarantee, so that he must swear about it too!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer from Step 12. If the lesson is 'land gets pulled in,' that lesson already exists in another משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A משנה usually does not repeat a rule taught somewhere else. Since the pulling-in rule already appears in another משנה, it seems this משנה would not need to teach it. That makes the answer in Step 12 look weak.

keyTerms.meaning: Pull in, bind: the oath on movable items extends to land
Property that serves as a guarantee, meaning land

phrases.english: What is it teaching us?
That property is pulled in?! We already learned it:

phrases.aramaic: זוֹקְקִין אֶת הַנְּכָסִים שֶׁיֵּשׁ לָהֶן אַחְרָיוּת,
phrases.english: Movable property pulls in property that serves as a guarantee,
phrases.notes: This is a משנה in קידושין. 'Property that serves as a guarantee' means land.

phrases.english: so that he must swear about it!

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן? זוֹקְקִין?! תְּנֵינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the explanation given in Step 12.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in Step 12 that the משנה mentioned land to teach the pulling-in rule.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: That rule is already taught in another משנה, so this משנה should not need to teach it again.

steps.title: This is the main source; the other משנה mentions it in passing
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that our משנה is the main place for the pulling-in rule. The other משנה only brings it along with other topics.
steps.simpleTranslation: This one is the main source. That one brought it along in passing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge: there is no repetition problem, because each משנה has a different role.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Our משנה is the main home of the pulling-in rule. The משנה in קידושין just mentions it while listing related rules. So the answer from Step 12 stands, and the proof from Step 11 stays rejected.
steps.whatToRemember: The vessels-and-land משנה does not prove that wheat-and-barley requires an oath. Land is mentioned to teach that it gets pulled into the oath, and this משנה is the main source for that rule.

phrases.english: This one is the main source,
that one brought it along in passing.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָא עִיקָּר, הָהִיא אַגַּב גְּרָרָא נַסְבַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 13.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Each source has a different role: one is the main teaching, the other is incidental.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Two משניות teaching the same rule would be a needless repeat.
steps.terutzMaskana: Our משנה is the main source; the other one mentions the rule only in passing.

steps.title: A ברייתא about an ox and a sheep
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבא בר ממל challenges רבי חייא בר אבא with a ברייתא. Claiming an ox and a sheep and admitting one of them requires an oath.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבא בר ממל objected to רבי חייא בר אבא: if he claimed an ox and the other admitted a sheep, or claimed a sheep and the other admitted an ox, he is exempt. If he claimed an ox and a sheep and the other admitted one of them, he must swear.
steps.whatsHappening: A new challenge comes against רבי חייא בר אבא, this time from a ברייתא that seems to say the opposite of his ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ox-and-sheep case is just like wheat and barley: two different items are claimed and one is admitted. The ברייתא says he must swear, while רבי חייא בר אבא reported in רבי יוחנן's name that there is no oath.

phrases.aramaic: אֵיתִיבֵיהּ רַבִּי אַבָּא בַּר מֶמֶל לְרַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא:
phrases.english: Rabbi Abba bar Memel objected to Rabbi Chiya bar Abba:
If he claimed an ox and the other admitted a sheep,
or a sheep and he admitted an ox: he is exempt.
If he claimed an ox and a sheep
and the other admitted one of them: he must swear.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֵיתִיבֵיהּ רַבִּי אַבָּא בַּר מֶמֶל לְרַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the proofs from the משנה are rejected, a new challenge comes from a ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי חייא בר אבא's report (Step 6) that claiming two items and admitting one gets no oath.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא openly says that claiming an ox and a sheep and admitting one requires an oath.

steps.title: The ברייתא follows רבן גמליאל
steps.stepSummary: רבי חייא בר אבא answers that the ברייתא follows רבן גמליאל, who requires an oath even when the admission is a different item from the claim.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Whose view is this? It is רבן גמליאל.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חייא בר אבא defends himself by saying the ברייתא follows a minority view, רבן גמליאל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבן גמליאל requires an oath even when the admission is a different kind of item from the claim, as Step 10 mentioned. If the ברייתא follows him, it does not reflect the view רבי יוחנן holds, so it does not contradict רבי חייא בר אבא.

phrases.english: He said to him:
Whose view is this? It is Rabban Gamliel.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 15.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Assigning the source to a specific תנא whose view is not followed.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא reflects the accepted view and contradicts רבי חייא בר אבא.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא follows רבן גמליאל, so it does not contradict רבי חייא בר אבא.

steps.title: Then the first case should also require an oath
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבא בר ממל pushes back: if the ברייתא follows רבן גמליאל, then even the first case (claimed an ox, admitted a sheep) should require an oath.
steps.simpleTranslation: If it is רבן גמליאל, then even the first part should require an oath too!
steps.whatsHappening: The answer from Step 16 is challenged. It does not fit the first half of the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבן גמליאל requires an oath even when the admission is a different item from the claim. But the first part of the ברייתא says that claiming an ox and admitting a sheep is exempt. So the ברייתא cannot follow רבן גמליאל.

keyTerms.meaning: The first part of a source

phrases.english: If it is Rabban Gamliel,
then even the first part should require an oath too!
phrases.notes: The first part is the case of claiming an ox and admitting a sheep, which the ברייתא calls exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי רַבָּן גַּמְלִיאֵל, אֲפִילּוּ רֵישָׁא נָמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in Step 16.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in Step 16 that the ברייתא follows רבן גמליאל.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבן גמליאל would require an oath even for claiming an ox and admitting a sheep, yet the ברייתא says that case is exempt.

steps.title: The ברייתא follows אדמון
steps.stepSummary: רבי חייא בר אבא drops the רבן גמליאל answer and says the ברייתא follows אדמון.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, whose view is this ברייתא? It is the view of אדמון.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חייא בר אבא answers the push-back from step 17 with a new author for the ברייתא: אדמון.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer 'רבן גמליאל' failed. רבן גמליאל would make even 'claimed an ox, admitted a sheep' liable, but the ברייתא calls that case exempt. אדמון fits both cases. He says the admission must come from the claim, so the first case is exempt. But in the jugs-of-oil case he makes someone liable who admits one item out of a combined claim, so 'claimed an ox and a sheep, admitted one' is liable.

keyTerms.meaning: A judge in ירושלים whose rulings appear in the משנה

phrases.english: Rather, whose view is this?
It is Admon.
phrases.notes: This is אדמון from the jugs-of-oil case back on 38b.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the רבן גמליאל answer that step 17 knocked down.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reassigning the author of the ברייתא
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא follows אדמון, who fits both of its cases.

steps.title: This is a set tradition from רבי יוחנן
steps.stepSummary: רבי חייא בר אבא says his answer is not a quick dodge. It is a fixed teaching he received from רבי יוחנן.
steps.simpleTranslation: I am not just pushing you off. It is a set teaching in the mouth of רבי יוחנן: this ברייתא follows אדמון.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חייא בר אבא backs up his answer with the authority of his teacher, רבי יוחנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His first answer (רבן גמליאל) was knocked down. So he wants to show that 'אדמון' is not just another guess. רבי יוחנן regularly taught that this ברייתא follows אדמון, which makes the answer solid.

keyTerms.meaning: I am just pushing you off (giving a weak answer)

steps.whatToRemember: The ox-and-sheep ברייתא follows אדמון, as רבי יוחנן taught.

phrases.english: And I am not just pushing you off,
rather, it is a set teaching
in the mouth of Rabbi Yochanan:
Whose view is this? It is Admon.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the answer of step 18 with a received tradition.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A fixed tradition of רבי יוחנן

steps.title: Admitting barley before the claim is finished
steps.stepSummary: The claimant began to claim wheat. The defendant jumped in first and admitted barley. If he did it as a trick he is liable to swear; if he meant it honestly he is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ענן said in the name of שמואל: He claimed wheat from him, and the other jumped in first and admitted barley. If he did it as a trick, he is liable. If he meant it honestly, he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new ruling. It is about a defendant who cuts off the claimant to admit something before the full claim is made.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Admitting barley when wheat is claimed is a different item, so normally there would be no oath. But if the defendant rushed in only to dodge an oath, before the claimant could add barley to his claim, his trick does not help him and he must swear. If he simply meant to answer, he stays exempt.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not read this as saying wheat and barley are the same item. The defendant is liable only because of his trick, not because barley counts as wheat.

phrases.english: Rav Anan said in the name of Shmuel:
He claimed wheat from him,
phrases.notes: He planned to claim both wheat and barley, but got cut off after the wheat.

phrases.english: and the other jumped in first and admitted barley to him —
if as a trick, he is liable.
If meaning it honestly, he is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new ruling about how closely the admission must match the claim.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A defendant who uses a trick to dodge the oath is still liable. One who answers honestly is exempt.

steps.title: Two needles: vessels of any value
steps.stepSummary: Someone claimed two needles and the defendant admitted one. He is liable to swear, because כלים count no matter how little they are worth.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב ענן said in the name of שמואל: He claimed two needles from him and he admitted one of them. He is liable. That is why the פסוק singles out vessels: to teach that they count at whatever value they have.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second ruling from the same speakers, about very cheap items.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally the claim must reach a minimum value for an oath. A needle is worth almost nothing. Even so, the oath applies, because the תורה mentions כלים separately to teach that vessels count no matter what they are worth.

keyTerms.meaning: For whatever they are (at any value)

phrases.english: And Rav Anan said in the name of Shmuel:
He claimed two needles from him
and he admitted one of them to him — he is liable.
That is why vessels were singled out
phrases.notes: This refers to the פסוק that says 'כסף או כלים' (שמות 22:6).

phrases.english: for whatever they are.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second, separate ruling from the same speakers.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Claims about כלים carry the oath even when the vessels are worth very little.
steps.whyThisMatters: It sets up the next step, where vessels of any value count but a single פרוטה of denial does not.

steps.title: Vessels and a פרוטה
steps.stepSummary: Someone claimed vessels and a פרוטה. If the defendant admits the vessels and denies the פרוטה, he is exempt. If he admits the פרוטה and denies the vessels, he is liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: He claimed vessels and a פרוטה. If he admitted the vessels and denied the פרוטה, he is exempt. If he admitted the פרוטה and denied the vessels, he is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא builds on the vessels rule with a pair of opposite cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The denied part is what the oath is about. A single denied פרוטה is too small to require an oath, so the first case is exempt. In the second case the denied part is vessels, which count at any value, and admitting even a פרוטה is enough of an admission, so he is liable.
steps.whatToRemember: Vessels count at any value. A denial of only a פרוטה does not bring an oath, but an admission of a פרוטה is enough.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
He claimed vessels and a peruta from him,
and he admitted the vessels and denied the peruta — he is exempt.
If he admitted the peruta and denied the vessels — he is liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the 'vessels of any value' rule from step 21 to a mixed claim.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Denying a פרוטה brings no oath. Denying vessels, after admitting a פרוטה, does bring an oath.

steps.title: One ruling follows רב and the other follows שמואל
steps.stepSummary: The two halves of the כלים-and-פרוטה case come from two different opinions. The exemption follows רב, and the liability follows שמואל.
steps.simpleTranslation: One ruling follows רב and one follows שמואל. The first follows רב, who says the denied part of a claim must be worth at least two silver coins. The second follows שמואל, who says that if someone claimed wheat and barley and the defendant admitted one of them, he is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the two halves of the last case come out differently. Each half follows a different אמורא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the defendant denies only the פרוטה, he is exempt, because רב requires the denied part to be worth at least two silver coins and a פרוטה is far less. If he admits the פרוטה and denies the כלים, he is liable, because שמואל holds that admitting one kind of item and denying another kind still counts as a partial admission.

keyTerms.meaning: The part of the claim that the defendant denies
Two silver coins (מָעוֹת), the smallest amount the denied part must reach according to רב
Wheat and barley, two different kinds of items

steps.whatToRemember: Denying only the פרוטה means exempt (רב: the denied part is too small). Admitting the פרוטה and denying the כלים means liable (שמואל: admitting one kind out of two kinds still counts).

phrases.english: One is like Rav, and one is like Shmuel.
One is like Rav, who says:
The denial of a claim must be two silver coins.
One is like Shmuel, who says:
If he claimed wheat and barley from him
and he admitted to him one of them, he is liable.
phrases.notes: It works the same way here: admitting the פרוטה and denying the כלים means admitting one kind and denying the other.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the two different outcomes in step 22 by tying each one to a different אמורא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the case between two authorities
steps.terutzHavaAmina: It looks inconsistent to exempt in one version of the case and make him liable in the other.
steps.terutzMaskana: Each half rests on a different principle: רב's minimum amount for the denied part, and שמואל's rule about admitting one kind out of two.

steps.title: Denying the whole claim still requires a rabbinic oath
steps.stepSummary: The משנה says that someone who denies the entire claim is exempt. רב נחמן adds that he still swears a שבועת היסת.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the claimant says "I have a מנה in your hand" and the defendant answers "You have nothing in my hand," the defendant is exempt. רב נחמן said: we still make him swear a שבועת היסת.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the משנה's case of a full denial, which is exempt from the Torah oath. רב נחמן then adds that the רבנן still require an oath.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By Torah law there is no oath without a partial admission, so a full denial is exempt. רב נחמן says this exemption covers only the Torah oath. The רבנן still require a שבועת היסת.

keyTerms.meaning: A sum of one hundred זוּז
A rabbinic oath for someone who denies the whole claim

steps.confusionAlert: The משנה's word פָּטוּר means exempt from the Torah oath. רב נחמן does not argue with the משנה. He adds a separate oath made by the רבנן.

phrases.english: "I have a maneh in your hand,"
"You have nothing in my hand": he is exempt.
Rav Nachman said:
And we make him swear an oath of heisset.
phrases.notes: This oath comes from the רבנן, not from the Torah.

steps.triggerLanguage: ״מָנֶה לִי בְּיָדֶךָ״, ״אֵין לְךָ בְּיָדִי״ – פָּטוּר. אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: the משנה's case of denying the entire claim.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Someone who denies the whole claim is exempt from the Torah oath but must swear a rabbinic שבועת היסת.

steps.title: Why impose this oath?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the reason behind רב נחמן's oath.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why the רבנן would make him swear when the Torah does not. This question sets up the answer that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is no partial admission here, so the Torah's reason for an oath is missing. The גמרא needs some other basis for doubting the defendant.

phrases.english: What is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reasoning behind רב נחמן's ruling in step 24.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The logic for imposing an oath on someone who denies the whole claim.

steps.title: People do not make claims for nothing
steps.stepSummary: We assume a person would not sue unless he really had something owed to him.
steps.simpleTranslation: There is a presumption that a person does not make a claim unless he has something against the other person.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains that the claimant himself gives us reason to doubt the denial. People do not usually sue for no reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the suspicion comes from the claimant, because we assume no one makes up a lawsuit out of thin air. That doubt is enough for the רבנן to require an oath, even without a partial admission.

keyTerms.meaning: A presumption, what we assume people normally do

phrases.english: There is a presumption that a person does not make a claim

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן יֵשׁ לוֹ עָלָיו.
phrases.english: unless he has something against him.

steps.triggerLanguage: חֲזָקָה אֵין אָדָם תּוֹבֵעַ, אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן יֵשׁ לוֹ עָלָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question asked in step 25.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A claim is usually not invented, so the denial is doubtful enough to require an oath.

steps.title: A borrower would not lie to his lender's face
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back with the opposite presumption: a borrower would not dare deny the whole debt to his lender's face.
steps.simpleTranslation: On the contrary! There is a presumption that a person does not act brazenly in front of his creditor.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב נחמן's reasoning with a presumption that points the other way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A person who owes money would feel too ashamed to tell his lender "you gave me nothing." So a full denial should actually make us believe the defendant, and he should not have to swear.

keyTerms.meaning: Acts brazenly, shamelessly lies to someone's face

phrases.english: On the contrary,
there is a presumption that a person does not act brazenly
in front of his creditor!

steps.triggerLanguage: אַדְּרַבָּה, חֲזָקָה אֵין אָדָם מֵעִיז פָּנָיו בִּפְנֵי בַּעַל חוֹבוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the reasoning given in step 26.
steps.kashyaTarget: The presumption that claims are not made for nothing, used to justify the שבועת היסת.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: An opposite presumption says a debtor would not lie outright to his lender, so a full denial should be believed.

steps.title: He is just stalling until he can pay
steps.stepSummary: Denying the whole debt is not brazen lying. The borrower is only putting the lender off until he has the money.
steps.simpleTranslation: He is just avoiding him. He thinks: once I have the money, I will pay him back.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. A full denial can come from a borrower who is stalling, not one who means to steal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The borrower does not see himself as boldly lying, because he plans to pay later. So the presumption against brazenness does not protect him, and the doubt that justifies the oath remains.

phrases.english: He is just avoiding him,
he thinks: until I have money,
and then I will repay him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge raised in step 27.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explaining the defendant's state of mind
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A full denial would be shameless lying, which a debtor would not do.
steps.terutzMaskana: A full denial can be temporary stalling, so it is not brazen and it remains suspicious.

steps.title: Proof: denying a loan does not make someone an invalid witness
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא rules that someone who denies a loan stays a valid witness, but someone who denies a deposit is invalid. This shows that denying a loan is treated as stalling, not stealing.
steps.simpleTranslation: Know that this is so, because רב אידי בר אבין said in the name of רב חסדא: someone who denies a loan is still fit to be a witness. Someone who denies a deposit is unfit to be a witness.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings support for the idea that a borrower who denies the debt is only stalling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If denying a loan were plain theft, the denier would lose his status as a witness. רב חסדא keeps him a valid witness, which shows the law sees him as someone putting off payment. Denying a deposit is different, so that person is invalid.

keyTerms.meaning: Know that this is so (introduces a proof)
A deposit, something left with someone for safekeeping

steps.whatToRemember: A full denial of a loan still gets a שבועת היסת (רב נחמן), because the borrower may be stalling rather than stealing. That is also why רב חסדא keeps him a valid witness.
steps.whyThisMatters: The שבועת היסת for someone who denies the whole claim became a standard part of how בית דין handles money claims.

phrases.english: Know that this is so,
as Rav Idi bar Avin said
that Rav Chisda said:
One who denies a loan is fit to be a witness.
One who denies a deposit is unfit to be a witness.

steps.triggerLanguage: תִּדַּע, דְּאָמַר רַב אִידִי בַּר אָבִין אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings support for the answer in step 28.
steps.raayaObject: That someone who denies a loan is only stalling, not stealing.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רב חסדא's ruling (through רב אידי בר אבין) that someone who denies a loan stays a valid witness, but someone who denies a deposit does not.

steps.title: A second version: the oath belongs to the later case
steps.stepSummary: רב חביבא teaches that רב נחמן's שבועת היסת was said about the second case: the borrower admitted the debt one day and the next day said he had already paid it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חביבא attaches it to the second case. Someone says, "I have a מנה in your hand," and the other says, "Yes." The next day he says, "Give it to me," and the other answers, "I already gave it to you." He is exempt. On this case רב נחמן said: we make him take a שבועת היסת.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second version of where רב נחמן's oath was said. Here it is about a borrower who admitted the debt and later claimed he had paid it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first version, the oath was about someone who denied the debt completely. In רב חביבא's version, the oath is only said about someone who first said 'yes, I owe' and then claimed he paid. The ruling stays the same: he is exempt by the basic law, but he still has to take a שבועת היסת. What changes is which case it is attached to.

keyTerms.meaning: Teaches, meaning he places the statement on a certain part of the משנה.
The later clause or second case of the משנה.
A sum of money, one hundred זוז.
"I gave it to you", a claim that he already paid.
An oath the חכמים added, given even when the basic law does not require an oath.

steps.confusionAlert: רב חביבא is not adding a new ruling. He is only saying that רב נחמן's same oath was said about the second case of the משנה, not the first.

phrases.english: Rav Chaviva teaches it on the latter clause:
phrases.notes: "It" means רב נחמן's statement about the oath, which we have been discussing.

phrases.english: "I have a maneh in your hand,"
and he said to him: "Yes";
the next day he said to him: "Give it to me,"
and he answered, "I gave it to you". He is exempt.
And Rav Nachman said:
We make him swear an oath of heses.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second version of where רב נחמן's oath applies, different from the version stated in step 24 and explained in steps 25-29.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A borrower who admitted the debt and later claims he paid it is exempt, but רב נחמן still makes him take a שבועת היסת.

steps.title: Comparing the versions: the first version covers the second case too
steps.stepSummary: Whoever places the oath on the first case (full denial) would surely also apply it to the second case (admitted, then claimed payment).
steps.simpleTranslation: Whoever teaches it on the first case would say it all the more so on the second case.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins comparing the two versions of רב נחמן's statement. It is setting up the next move, which will explain what the second version means for the first case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If even a borrower who denied everything must swear, then a borrower who admitted the debt and only claims he paid must surely swear too. So the first version includes both cases. Whether רב חביבא's version also covers the first case is taken up on the next amud.

keyTerms.meaning: The first clause or first case of the משנה.
All the more so, a stronger case built from a weaker one.
The one who teaches, meaning the opinion that places it there.

phrases.english: The one who teaches it on the first clause,
phrases.notes: The first clause is the case where the borrower says "You have nothing with me" and denies the whole debt.

phrases.english: all the more so on the latter clause;

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאן דְּמַתְנֵי אַרֵישָׁא כׇּל שֶׁכֵּן אַסֵּיפָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts comparing the first version with רב חביבא's version from step 30, showing that the first version also covers the second case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If an oath is required when the borrower denies the whole debt, it is surely required when he admitted the debt and only claims he paid.
